title: How to identify content gaps for AI visibility
content:
Learning how to identify content gaps for AI visibility starts with a question that traditional content gap analysis doesn’t always answer: where could a brand contribute something useful to an AI-generated answer, but isn’t being mentioned or cited?
With AI and SEO trends changing how people discover brands, finding a content gap isn’t always as simple as identifying a missing article. A company might already have a relevant page that AI search engines aren’t citing, or an AI assistant might mention the brand while relying on another website for supporting information. Creating more content without understanding what’s missing may not solve the problem.
This guide walks through how to use prompt-tracking data and existing content to identify AI visibility gaps, review competing sources, and decide what to do next.
An AI visibility content gap is a relevant information need, represented by a prompt or group of prompts, for which a brand is absent from AI-generated answers, lacks supporting citations, or does not have content that adequately addresses the question.
Traditional content gap analysis typically compares a website’s keyword coverage and search performance with competing websites. It helps marketers identify topics and queries that competitors rank for, but their own websites do not. AI SEO uses artificial intelligence to support traditional SEO tasks, such as keyword research, content analysis, and optimization. Both approaches — traditional SEO and AI-assisted SEO — focus on improving a website’s performance in traditional search results.
AI visibility analysis examines a different set of outcomes. A page can rank well in Google and still be absent from a ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity response. And, to add to the complexity, an AI assistant may mention a brand without directing readers to the brand’s website at all. That difference makes it important to understand three types of AI visibility gaps:
For marketers, treat these categories as diagnostic rather than mutually exclusive. A page may cover the right topic but lack both a direct answer and sufficient evidence to support a citation. The objective is to identify what is missing from the answer ecosystem, not simply what is missing from a content calendar.
An AI mention occurs when an answer names a brand, product, or company. An AI citation occurs when the answer provides a source reference or link supporting information in the response. For marketers, understanding these differences in outcomes makes it easier to identify content opportunities.
For example, an AI assistant answering “What are the best project management tools for agencies?” might recommend a particular platform but cite an independent review site for its pricing, integrations, or suitability. The brand has achieved mention visibility, but its own content is not necessarily being used as the supporting source.
A citation to the brand’s website provides a different signal. A citation to the brand’s website means the assistant has surfaced that website as a source for the answer. However, a citation alone does not establish that the assistant recommended the brand, that a reader clicked the link, or that the answer generated revenue.
Pro tip: Record mentions and citations separately. A brand can be mentioned in an AI answer without citing a single piece of its own content as a source. That is a completely different situation with a completely different fix, and combining them into a single visibility metric can conceal whether the opportunity involves brand inclusion, source selection, or both.
An AI visibility content gap analysis follows four steps: collect relevant prompt data, classify mentions and citations, map findings to existing content, and prioritize gaps by business relevance and the work required to address them. The content gap analysis process begins by reviewing the answers AI platforms currently produce, rather than assuming which articles a company should publish. Here’s what to do.
Prompt tracking establishes where a brand appears in AI-generated answers and where relevant questions produce no brand mention or citation.
Start with a defined set of prompts representing the questions prospective customers ask during discovery, evaluation, and purchase. Group prompts by topic and intent so that individual wording variations do not become separate content projects.
I use HubSpot AEO to identify groups of prompts related to the services I offer through Cassie Clark Marketing. HubSpot’s AEO tool tracks prompts across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, showing how a brand appears in answers alongside competitors and citations. The marketing team can then use those observations to identify which prompts or topic areas need a closer look.
Using Cassie Clark Marketing as an example, HubSpot AEO suggested several prompts related to answer-engine optimization consulting:
These prompts reflect a related need (finding an answer-engine optimization partner), but they approach that need from different angles. One asks for services to compare, another focuses on selection criteria, and the third introduces a specific operational requirement.
Grouping related prompts helps identify the broader topic a brand needs to cover without treating every variation as a separate content opportunity. The next step is to examine the AI-generated answers and determine whether existing content addresses those needs, and where coverage may be missing.
The next step is to record what happens when an AI assistant answers each prompt. Run the prompts through an AI answer engine and note which brands appear in the response and which websites are cited as sources.
I like to use a spreadsheet to keep track of these observations. For example, when I tested the prompt “Which AI search visibility audit service suits a scaling B2B SaaS startup?” ChatGPT recommended Profound, Otterly, Scrunch, and Peec AI. Cassie Clark Marketing was absent from the answer, and the cited sources focused on AI visibility software.
I would record that observation in my spreadsheet, along with the prompt, platform, date, brands mentioned, and cited sources. From there, I can use the following outcomes to identify what needs a closer look:
The goal of this step is a shortlist of prompt groups with a clearly documented visibility pattern. The classification system prevents teams from treating every missing citation as a reason to write another article.
For instance, if a brand is regularly mentioned but a third-party directory supplies its feature information, the immediate task may be to review the brand’s product documentation. A new thought-leadership article might do little to address that particular gap.
Prompt-to-page mapping determines whether the company already has content that answers the questions surfaced by prompt tracking. For each priority prompt group, search the company’s website and content inventory for pages that address the underlying information need. Include product pages, documentation, comparison pages, case studies, research, and relevant blog posts. Assess each candidate page against four questions.
Consider the prompt, “Which AI search visibility audit service suits a scaling B2B SaaS startup?”
When I tested this prompt, ChatGPT recommended several AI visibility software platforms, including Profound, Otterly, Scrunch, and Peec AI. Cassie Clark Marketing didn’t appear in the answer, even though I offer AI search visibility audits for startups and enterprise brands.
The response revealed a potential content opportunity beyond simply getting my brand mentioned. ChatGPT treated the question primarily as a request for software rather than a consultant-led service. The cited sources were also comparisons of AI visibility tools.
My existing audit services page clearly explains who the service is for and what it includes. However, the answer I captured focused on software rather than consultant-led audits, even though the prompt specifically asked about audit services.
With that in mind, I would consider creating content that explains the difference between an AI visibility monitoring platform and a consultant-led audit, including what each provides and when a scaling B2B SaaS company might need one, the other, or both.
The goal is to address an information need that my existing services page doesn’t fully cover, rather than creating another page simply because my brand was missing from the answer.
Pro tip: Before assigning a content project, confirm that the company actually offers the product or service the prompt asks about. A missing mention could point to a content gap, but it could also reveal a capability gap, a positioning issue, or a question that isn’t relevant to the business.
Record the most relevant existing URL for each prompt group, if one exists. If no page adequately addresses the question, consider whether new content could fill that gap before adding another article to the calendar.
Content gaps should be prioritized according to business relevance, the strength of the observed visibility pattern, the nature of the missing information, and the effort required to address it. To decide which content gaps to tackle first, look at two things:
For Cassie Clark Marketing, the prompt about AI search visibility audit services for scaling B2B SaaS startups is closely aligned with my target audience and the services I offer. The answer also suggests an information gap worth exploring: it recommends monitoring software without clearly addressing consultant-led audits.
Creating a resource that explains the difference would take more work than updating a paragraph on my services page, but the topic is directly relevant to prospective clients evaluating their options. I would prioritize it as a potential new content project.
Pro tip: Be sure to also look at the third-party sources ChatGPT cited. Since those sources focus on software comparisons, there may be an opportunity to contribute a consultant’s perspective to relevant industry publications. That would be a separate effort from creating content for a brand website, but both initiatives could help address the information gap identified in the answer.
Analyzing AI and search results helps marketers identify the information, evidence, and source characteristics present in answers where their brand is absent or not cited. For each prioritized prompt group:
Don’t copy a competing article. The objective here is to understand what the answer requires and whether the company’s existing content satisfies that need. Look for recurring patterns:
Then compare those findings with the page mapped to that prompt.
For example, with Cassie Clark Marketing, if an AI answer explains how an enterprise content team can build an AI visibility strategy, but my services page only says I offer AI search consulting, I may need to explain what that work looks like for a large team. That could mean adding details about the discovery process, how I work with internal stakeholders, and what the team can expect from the engagement.
Extractability describes how clearly a page presents information that can be identified, understood, and reused in an answer. Improving extractability requires making the useful information accessible without forcing readers — or retrieval systems — to reconstruct it from vague or scattered statements. Here are a few ways to improve an existing page.
The goal is a page that communicates clearly to its intended reader. Better structure supports that goal, but structure alone doesn’t establish that an AI platform will retrieve or cite the page.
Original information gives a page something substantive to contribute beyond a summary of material available elsewhere. Depending on the topic, that contribution may come from:
Originality should help answer the reader’s question. A proprietary statistic with no explanation of how it was collected may be less useful than a real example that shows exactly how a user can apply the information.
For research-led content, include the source, date, sample size, and methodology. For client examples, confirm permission and remove confidential information. When incorporating expert commentary from an interview, preserve the guest’s intended meaning rather than stretching a quote to support a broader claim.
While adding original information can’t guarantee an AI citation, it makes the content more useful and gives readers a clearer basis for evaluating its claims.
Once a gap has been identified, the next step is to determine whether an existing page can address it or new content is needed. A missing brand mention alone isn’t enough to make that decision.
Before creating a new page, check whether the topic belongs within an existing resource. Several closely related articles may fragment a useful explanation across URLs without addressing the underlying question more effectively.
After publishing, keep a record of what changed, including the URL, the gap the update addressed, the publication date, and the prompt group being tracked. This makes it easier to measure the results over time.
Pro tip: Recommendations in HubSpot’s AEO tool may help teams identify potential actions, such as creating new content, updating existing pages, or fixing technical gaps. Take a second to review those recommendations against the existing content inventory and the underlying prompt evidence before assigning work to the content team.
Track how often the brand is mentioned, how often its content is cited, and how well AI-generated answers address the prompts being monitored to measure whether content updates are making a difference.
Keep in mind that AI-generated answers can vary from one run to the next. Competitor activity and platform changes can also affect visibility, so an increase in mentions or citations doesn’t necessarily mean a content update caused it.
Start with a baseline measurement from before the update, then track the same prompt groups across the same platforms using consistent measurement methods. This makes it easier to spot changes over time without drawing conclusions from a single response. Here are a few AEO metrics to track.
Brand mention presence measures how often a brand appears in answers to the prompts being tracked. The calculation is straightforward: Mention presence = Answers mentioning the brand ÷ Total tracked answers × 100
For accurate comparisons, use the same method each time. For example, decide whether each observation represents a single prompt run or a unique prompt, and stick with that approach.
If mention presence increases after a content update, look at the actual answers to see how the brand is being discussed. A passing mention or an inaccurate description may not be the result the team was hoping for.
For prompts where the brand is still absent, review the relevant pages to see whether they clearly explain how the company relates to the topic or use case.
Citation presence measures how often a brand’s own content is cited in the answers being tracked. The calculation is: Citation presence = Answers citing at least one brand-owned URL ÷ Total tracked answers × 100
Citation presence measures the share of answers that cite the brand, not the total number of citations. If one answer cites three pages from the same website, it still counts as one answer with a brand citation.
When citation presence changes, look at which pages are being cited and how the AI assistant is using them. More citations may mean the brand’s content is appearing as a source more often, but the context of those citations matters, too.
For prompts where the brand is mentioned but its content isn’t cited, compare the brand’s pages with the sources the assistant uses. Look for information that may be missing, explanations that could be clearer, or supporting evidence that could be added.
AI share of voice measures how often a brand appears compared with other brands across the prompts being tracked. There are two ways to calculate it, depending on what’s being measured.
Entity-based share of voice and citation-based share of voice measure different things, so it’s important to choose one and use it consistently.
When share of voice changes, look beyond the overall percentage. Check which brands are appearing, how they’re being discussed, and which prompt groups are driving the change. An increase in one topic doesn’t necessarily mean the brand is gaining visibility across every topic being tracked.
AI-referred traffic can help show whether AI search visibility is translating into website visits. When referral data is available, look at which pages visitors land on, how they engage with the site, and whether they take actions such as submitting a form or becoming a customer.
HubSpot’s traffic analytics tool classifies visits from AI assistants as AI Referrals, and contact records can carry that source, so teams can connect AI-referred visits to the contacts they create.
But that data only captures part of the picture. Some AI-driven visits may not be identified as referrals, and someone who discovers a brand through an AI answer might return later through another channel. Referral and CRM data are best used alongside mention and citation tracking to understand how AI visibility relates to business outcomes, rather than to attribute a sale to a specific content update.
Pro tip: Keep a log of content updates, major product changes, and changes to the tracking process. Review trends across multiple observations instead of assuming that the latest content edit caused a change in AI visibility.
The most common mistakes in AI visibility content gap analysis come from treating observations as instructions. A missing mention does not automatically justify a new page, and a cited competitor does not automatically reveal what the brand should publish.
As an AI search visibility consultant, I’ve seen how easy it is for brands to focus on the most obvious gaps rather than the ones that actually need attention. Here are a few mistakes to avoid when deciding what content to create or update.
A single prompt can produce different answers from one run to the next. If every missing mention triggers a new article or content update, the editorial calendar can quickly become a reaction to normal AI answer variation.
Instead, group related prompts and look for patterns over time. Before assigning work, consider how relevant the underlying question is to the business. If the results are inconsistent, keep tracking the prompt until there’s enough information to make a decision.
Not every visibility gap deserves the same attention. A brand might be missing from answers to a broad, popular question but appear regularly in answers to more specific questions its prospective customers are asking.
Focus on prompts that relate to the company’s services, target audience, and buying decisions. Review the wording of each prompt and the answers it produces to make sure the content opportunity is relevant to the people the business wants to reach.
Making content easy for AI assistants to extract shouldn’t come at the expense of making it useful for readers. A page filled with short definitions, repetitive headings, and quick answers might be easy to scan, but it can leave out the examples and context people need to understand the topic.
Use headings and formatting to organize the information, not replace it. Keep the explanations, firsthand experience, and details that make the content worth reading in the first place.
Pro tip: AI-generated content can help with drafting and organizing a page, but it still needs a human review to check the facts, assess the sources, and make sure the final piece answers a question readers actually have.
Content gap analysis gets easier when there’s a consistent way to track prompts, review AI-generated answers, and decide what to do next.
A spreadsheet is a good place to start tracking for content gap analysis. It brings prompt data, existing content, and proposed updates into one place so the team can see which gaps need attention and which can wait. Here’s what to include in the audit and how to turn the findings into a content brief.
An AEO gap audit checklist helps organize the findings from each prompt group and connect them to a potential content update. Set up two tabs in the spreadsheet: one to record individual prompt responses and another to summarize the gaps identified across related prompts. Use one row per prompt group in the summary tab, and keep individual observations in the first tab so changes between runs don’t get lost. Set up the AEO audit gap checklist like this:
Once a gap has been prioritized, the next step is to turn the findings into a content brief. The brief should give the writer enough context to understand the customer’s question, what the existing content is missing, and what the finished page needs to accomplish. Open a new word processing document and use this template:
The most important part of the brief is explaining why the content needs to be created or updated. A list of prompts might tell a writer what people are asking, but it doesn’t explain what’s missing from the existing content or how the new piece should address that gap.
HubSpot’s free AI Search Grader provides a starting point for understanding how AI answer engines represent a brand. AI Search Grader evaluates areas such as brand recognition, sentiment, presence quality, share of voice, and market position.
For example, if AI Search Grader’s results suggest that a brand has limited visibility in AI-generated answers, the next step would be to examine the specific prompts, sources, and existing content behind that result. That initial assessment can help identify areas worth investigating before moving into a more detailed content gap analysis.
HubSpot’s AEO tool helps marketers track how their brands appear in AI-generated answers across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, including the prompts being monitored, brand mentions, citations, and competitor visibility. For content gap analysis, this can help identify prompts where a brand is missing, appears without a citation, or is described differently from competing brands. The next step is to compare those findings with the company’s existing content:
That review helps determine whether marketers need to update an existing page, create something new, or address a different issue altogether.
For Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise users, the AEO tool can also use CRM data to inform prompt suggestions. HubSpot’s SEO marketing software can add to this analysis by surfacing SEO recommendations, topic opportunities, and organic search performance.
Together, HubSpot’s tools can help marketers understand how their pages perform in traditional search and how their brand and content appear in AI-generated answers.
Start with a full content gap analysis to establish a baseline. From there, revisit it when priorities shift, the content strategy changes, or an important topic needs another look. After publishing or updating a page, continue tracking the relevant prompts to see whether any changes in visibility hold up over time. How often this happens will depend on the number of prompts being tracked, how frequently content is updated, and how much time the team has to act on the findings.
Start with the platforms your audience is most likely to use. ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Google’s AI Overviews are good places to start, but the right mix depends on where prospective customers go to research options and make decisions.
Review results from each platform separately before combining them. The same prompt can produce different answers and citations across platforms, and their measurement capabilities may differ.
Not every gap needs to become a content project. If a prompt has little to do with the target audience, asks about a service the company doesn’t offer, or only shows a missing mention in one or two responses, it may be worth setting aside.
The same goes for a gap that would take significant time and resources to address but has limited relevance to the business. Keep a record of why the gap was deprioritized so the team can revisit it if priorities or circumstances change.
Website analytics aren’t required to track brand mentions, citations, or AI share of voice. These metrics can be measured by monitoring a consistent set of prompts and recording the answers each platform produces. For each observation, capture the prompt, platform, date, answer, and cited sources. This provides a record of how the brand appears in the answers being tracked, even when AI-referred website traffic can’t be identified.
Keep in mind that prompt tracking measures visibility within the selected sample. It doesn’t show how many people saw those answers or visited the website afterward.
Start small. Choose a handful of prompts that relate directly to the company’s services and the questions prospective customers are asking. Track where the brand is mentioned or cited, review the sources AI assistants use, and compare those findings with the company’s existing content. Look for one clear gap that can be addressed by updating a relevant page rather than taking on a large content project right away.
Record the baseline before making the update, then revisit the same prompts afterward to see what changes.
Identifying content gaps for AI visibility starts with connecting what AI assistants say to real customer questions and the information a company can credibly provide. Prompt tracking shows where a brand is absent or isn’t being cited, while reviewing existing pages helps determine whether the issue is missing information, unclear explanations, insufficient evidence, or something content alone can’t fix.
The advice I give each of my clients is to resist the urge to create content every time a brand is missing from an AI answer. Focus on the gaps that matter to the business and where there’s a genuine opportunity to provide a better answer.
HubSpot AEO can support that process by bringing prompt, visibility, competitor, and citation data into the analysis. For teams beginning to build an AEO practice, HubSpot’s Early-Signs Guide to AEO offers a next step, with early strategies, page-level best practices, and survey data on how other marketers are approaching AEO.

title: Which AI prompts should you track? A practical guide
content:
For most teams, the answer to “which prompts should I track?” is this: track a representative sample of branded, unbranded, and competitor prompts across buyer stages, personas, and priority markets. Don’t fall into the trap of tracking everything.
Remember: buyers don’t query answer engines the way they query Google. A prompt often reads like a brief. Prompts often include details like team size, budget, location, and follow-up questions that all reshape the answer. Faced with that variation, marketers either track everything and drown in noise or fall back on branded queries that inflate visibility metrics.
This guide aims to help marketers build an effective prompt tracking set. The guide explains choosing and balancing prompts as well as scoring, maintaining, and turning visibility and citation findings into content decisions.
According to Responsive research , 56% of tech buyers are turning to generative AI to build vendor shortlists. Answer engines increasingly drive which brands buyers consider before they ever visit a website.
Tracking prompts shows marketers whether their brand appears where buyers are asking, how it’s described, and which competitors and sources are winning those answers instead.
Think about prompts in three broad categories: branded, unbranded, and competitor.
Branded prompts include the company or product name, such as “What is [Brand]?” or “Does [Brand] integrate with Salesforce?”
Important note: In the same way that a brand will rank for its branded keyword in traditional SEO, answer engines should always mention the brand here, so presence isn’t the metric. Branded prompts protect brand accuracy in AI answers. For branded prompts, the focus is sentiment and accuracy.
Unbranded prompts describe a problem or category without naming any company, such as “best project management software for agencies” or “how to reduce client onboarding time.” Unbranded solution-seeking prompts measure discovery-stage visibility. Unbranded prompts usually reveal the biggest gaps and should make up the largest share of a prompt set.
In my experience, unbranded prompts deserve the same priority as unbranded keywords in traditional SEO. Search teams often judge search performance by branded demand, but search teams and stakeholders must understand that nonbranded search plays a critical role in performance as well.
Increasing brand visibility is mostly the job of PR, brand marketing, and wider visibility efforts. Search supports that work, but a search team’s core role is to reach buyers who are still discovering their options and don’t yet know which brands to consider. In AI search, unbranded prompts are where that discovery happens. Unbranded prompts are the clearest measure of whether answer engine optimization (AEO) is reaching new buyers, tying visibility as directly as possible to a search team’s efforts.
Competitor prompts reveal where rivals appear during evaluation. Competitor prompts name one or more rivals, such as “Is [Competitor] good for remote teams?” or “alternatives to [Competitor].” Answers to these prompts show which brands answer engines consider as the category’s default options, and whether the brand appears as a credible alternative.
Pro Tip: If possible, track prompts for three to five direct competitors. Keep the focus on competitors who have solid marketing strategies and perform well online.
Ideally, marketers will track prompts that fall under all three categories of branded, unbranded, and competitor.
Using dedicated tools for prompt tracking, instead of manual checks, makes spotting trends more manageable for marketers. HubSpot’s AEO tool gives marketers one place to monitor prompts and track brand visibility across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. Teams can compare how often competitors appear on the same prompts, review which sources answer engines cite, and turn findings into clear, prioritized recommendations.
For Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise customers, AEO is included and uses CRM data to suggest prompts to track, rather than relying on generic industry templates. HubSpot’s AEO tool is also available standalone for $50/month (25 prompts included).
A balanced prompt mix can look slightly different for different businesses. One thing that stays the same is that a balanced prompt mix puts most tracking effort where visibility is uncertain, and buyers are still deciding. Search marketers can make the biggest difference in this uncertain visibility phase through prompt balancing.
Branded search should always show the brand anyway. Conversions on branded search should always be strong, as this is the type of search people make when they’ve made their decision.
Paid search data from my boutique search marketing agency, forank , shows the relationship between branded search and conversions clearly. My business partner, Leigh Buttrey , runs paid advertising for a leading London catering company, and I manage the company’s SEO and AEO efforts. Paid campaigns show exactly which searches drive conversions and provide insight into user behavior where keywords are concerned. This is data that SEO teams don’t have, because Google doesn’t provide conversion data for organic search. Because it’s hard to know which keywords actually drive conversions, SEO can borrow from paid campaign data. A keyword that performs well for paid search will, in theory, perform well for organic SEO.
This year, our catering company’s branded campaign generated 223 conversions at a 4.20% conversion rate. Branded search accounts for around 46% of all conversions from the company’s search campaigns. The data tells a story about how customers come back and search for the business by name once they’re ready to act. We see this pattern across many accounts. Vendor decisions are often made during the research phase, and the branded search is just the last step. That’s why visibility in unbranded, research-stage prompts matters most.
Start with a ratio of queries split between unbranded, competitor, and branded. Get a feel for the data and whether it’s suitable for the marketing campaigns running.
The unbranded, competitor, and branded categories are solid but broad. Next, make prompt tracking more useful by tracking prompts by persona or ideal client profile (ICP). Tracking by persona or ICP helps marketers ensure they’re reaching every major decision-maker, which is especially important in complex B2B settings. For example, one marketing team may need stakeholder buy-in from a Chief Finance Officer (CFO), an Operations Lead, and the end user.
A CFO might ask for “software that shortens month-end close,” while an Operations Lead asks how to “automate invoice approvals.” These audiences probably want the same product, and putting your company’s product in front of both audiences increases the chances of your brand appearing in boardrooms when vendor decisions are being made. Aim to cover each priority persona.
Pro tip: Review the prompt mix regularly. Complete the first review after the first month. If branded prompts consistently return accurate, positive answers, consider moving those slots to unbranded or competitor prompts where there’s more to learn.
Awareness prompts are broad and problem-focused. The buyer is trying to understand a challenge. They’re not choosing a vendor. Answer engines tend to explain concepts and cite educational content, often without naming brands. Here’s an example of Google’s AI Overviews (AIO) for an awareness query:
Decision prompts are narrow and packed with constraints such as budget, integrations, team size, or contract terms. Answers usually name a few vendors, so these searches influence the buyer’s shortlist. Here’s an example of Google AIO for a decision query:
Any of the three tools mentioned in the AIO has a good chance of a website click or making the buyer shortlist.
Tracking prompts by buyer journey connects visibility to how buyers actually move toward a purchase. Buyer-journey prompt sets cover awareness, consideration, evaluation, and decision intent.
Most of the prompt set belongs in the consideration and evaluation stages, where shortlists form. Awareness prompts are worth a smaller share to check whether answer engines use the brand’s content as a source, even when they don’t name the brand.
According to 6sense’s 2025 Buyer Experience Report , B2B buyers evaluated an average of 5.1 vendors, up from 4.5 the year before. In previous years, each additional vendor on a shortlist added about two months to the buying cycle. This time, cycles actually shortened by just over a month. Buyers are comparing more options in less time, so every stage of research carries more comparison questions, and each one is a chance for a brand to make or miss the shortlist.
After an initial answer, buyers using answer engines will narrow down with follow-ups like:
A brand that doesn’t cover the details can appear in the first answer and disappear once the buyer adds constraints.
Since tracking tools ‌run each prompt as a standalone question, marketers must write follow-ups as complete prompts with context. The same principles behind effective ChatGPT prompts , including clear context, a specific role, and defined constraints, apply to writing prompts worth tracking.
For example, instead of tracking “Which is cheapest?” track “What’s the most affordable project management tool for agencies with built-in time tracking?” Add standalone follow-ups that reflect the most common next questions.
Pro tip: The best follow-up prompts come from questions sales teams hear repeatedly in discovery calls and demos, because those reflect the real objections buyers have before they commit.
If your prompt tracking tool allows, as HubSpot AEO does, keep each root prompt and its follow-ups in the same tracking group . Reporting then shows exactly where in the conversation the brand drops out. This can point to the specific content gap to fix, such as missing pricing information or undocumented integrations.
Search marketing efforts have the same goal as other teams in the company: they need to make money for the business. Therefore, the prompts to start tracking first should be tied to revenue.
Start by identifying prompts that drive clicks and revenue. I like to reverse-engineer which landing pages are being clicked. Landing pages receiving clicks from AEO are clearly working for the business. Landing pages that also convert are clearly working. Sometimes, landing pages have a clear angle, like a specific feature or audience. It’s not an exact science, but marketing should be able to make some educated guesses on the type of prompts that are leading to the landing page’s visibility.
Sales and customer service teams are a valuable source. The questions that sales teams hear repeatedly in discovery calls and demos, such as “How long does implementation take?”, “Will it work with our existing systems?”, or “What happens to our data if we switch?” reflect the real concerns buyers need resolved before they commit. Buyers increasingly ask answer engines these same questions before they ever speak to a sales rep, so turning recurring objections into tracked prompts shows whether AI answers address those concerns, and whether they point buyers toward the brand or a competitor. Structured voice-of-the-customer methodologies , such as reviewing call recordings or tagging common objections in support tickets, make it easier to spot which questions come up most often.
Featured resource: 51 AI Prompts for Sales Teams to Use [+Expert Tips]
Prompts are so varied and subjective that it’s easy to become overwhelmed tracking many of them. Instead, start smaller, then build the prompts over time.
A starting set of 25 to 50 prompts is enough to spot patterns without creating noise. HubSpot AEO’s free trial covers 25 prompts across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini, a useful benchmark for a first set. Expand once the first month of data shows which topics need deeper coverage.
Pro tip: Before finalizing a first set, run a quick baseline. HubSpot’s free AI Search Grader is a one-time diagnostic that scores how ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity characterize a brand across five dimensions: sentiment, presence quality, brand recognition, share of voice, and market position. Marketers can run it for their own brand, then for each key competitor using the same location and category, to compare how sentiment and share of voice differ across the market. Weak scores point to where tracking should start. Low presence quality suggests unbranded category prompts, while weak sentiment suggests branded prompts around the issues driving it.
Here’s an example of what AI Search Grader says about HubSpot’s opportunities:
AI Search Grader specifically shows “Growth Areas.” These areas could inform decisions about marketing campaigns and prompts to target. Across two core answer engine platforms (OpenAI and Perplexity), enhanced/advanced analytics are listed as a growth opportunity, and in Gemini, AI and automation capabilities are listed. There’s some crossover between these features, so teams could create content that addresses these areas and therefore increase visibility. Tracking prompts related to these topics would then make sense.
Query fan-out is the process answer engines use to break a single prompt into multiple related searches behind the scenes. Google has described AI Mode and AIO working this way : “While responses are being generated, our advanced models identify more supporting web pages, allowing us to display a wider and more diverse set of helpful links associated with the response than with a classic web search, enabling new opportunities for exploration."
A prompt like “best project management tool for a small agency with client billing” might fan out into separate searches on agency project management tools, billing features, pricing, and reviews. The engine then combines what it finds into one answer.
Fan-out explains why tracking every phrasing of a question adds little value. Ten different wordings of the same question often trigger overlapping sub-queries and pull from many of the same sources. Clustering groups those variations by underlying intent, so one or two representative prompts can stand in for the whole cluster.
For example, “best project management tool for agencies” and “top agency project management software” belong in the same cluster. Clustering is best practice for three reasons.
CRM data shows who buys, why they buy, and who the business loses deals to, making it one of the most reliable sources for prompt selection. Yet CRM data is often overlooked because most standalone AEO tools have no connection to a company’s customer data. Without the link between AEO tool and CRM data, teams are effectively guessing at which prompts matter. The risk is that marketers end up falling back on generic category questions that may not reflect their real buyers.
For teams working out how to use CRM data to find prompts to track, the goal is to turn real customer patterns into prompts. Here’s how to discover the prompts your marketing team should track based on data within the CRM.
Look for patterns in recent closed-won deals such as the industries, company sizes, regions, and use cases that appear most often. Each pattern becomes a set of unbranded prompts written from that buyer’s perspective. If mid-sized healthcare companies make up a large share of new revenue, prompts like “best patient scheduling software for multi-location clinics” deserve a place in the set.
Lost deals show where the brand is losing ground. Competitors named in closed-lost records belong in the competitor prompt set, and recurring loss reasons such as price, missing integrations, or ease of use point to evaluation prompts worth tracking.
Not every segment deserves equal coverage. Give more prompts to segments with the highest deal value, shortest sales cycles, or strongest retention, and fewer to segments that generate leads but rarely convert.
Pro tip: Revisit CRM-based prompts whenever the business enters a new market, launches a product, or sees a shift in who’s buying. The prompt set should follow the customer base.
HubSpot’s AEO tool connects to CRM data from day one for Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise customers. Prompt suggestions are based on that data, not generic industry templates, so marketers start with prompts tailored to their business and can add their own. As CRM data grows, suggestions stay aligned with how the customer base is changing.
Keywords and FAQs that already perform in traditional search are one of the fastest ways to build a prompt set, because they show proven demand and topics where the brand already has authority. The job is to turn short, keyword-style searches into the longer, context-rich questions buyers ask answer engines.
Google Search Console shows which queries already drive impressions and clicks. The most useful queries for prompt tracking are long-tail queries, which often reveal a problem or hint at who is searching, and question-style queries, which closely resemble how people phrase prompts. Exporting Google Search Console (GSC) data and sorting queries by word count is a quick way to surface them.
A keyword becomes a useful prompt when it includes details a real buyer would add, such as role, company size, constraint, or goal. Use CRM data to build the audience and understand the details.
Keep the core topic of the keyword intact, so prompt results can still be compared with organic performance for the same topic.
Featured resource: 70 AI prompt examples for marketers to use today
FAQs are already written as questions, which makes them easy to convert. Strong sources include on-site FAQ sections, People Also Ask results, support tickets, and pre-sales questions. Add buyer context to generic FAQs, and prioritize the questions tied to purchase decisions, such as pricing, integrations, and implementation, over purely definitional ones.
Teams that already organize content into topic clusters have a ready-made structure for prompts. Each pillar topic can become a prompt cluster, with the subtopics informing the individual prompts. This keeps prompt reporting aligned with content strategy, so a visibility gap in a cluster points straight to the pillar or supporting pages that need work.
Marketing Hub’s SEO tools make topic and prompt clustering easier for HubSpot users. They surface prioritized recommendations for optimizing site pages, suggest topics that build search authority, and integrate with Google Search Console so teams can see how queries perform, including impressions and click-through rate. That query and cluster data is a practical starting point for translating proven keywords into conversational prompts.
The right setup depends on the individual business because there are many variables, such as where buyers research, which markets drive revenue, and how much variation the team can manage in analysis and reporting.
According to HubSpot’s 2026 State of AEO Report, consumers’ preferred platforms are ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews. These two platforms are a good place to start; however, every business should try to find out where their specific audiences are searching. For most businesses, there are three to four core platforms, including:
If teams want to discover exactly which platforms are driving traffic to a website, set up a report on Data Studio (formerly called Looker Studio) that pulls information from Google Analytics showing the source and the landing page visit.
GA4 specialist Kyle Rushton-McGregor taught me how to create a report in Data Studio . Here’s what my Data Studio report looks like:
I can see that ChatGPT is sending the most traffic through September, followed by Google. This indicates that AEO is working for my client, but it’s important to consider that a brand will only get traffic from an AI source where it has brand visibility. GA4 can only show the click, not the missing opportunities.
Answer engines can return different brands, sources, and pricing depending on where a buyer is located. Tracking prompts by location shows whether a brand appears in the markets that matter most.
Start with the markets that drive the most revenue or growth. Track the core prompt set in the primary market and a smaller, localized subset in secondary markets. Localized prompts should reflect how buyers there actually ask, including spelling, currency, and local regulations or competitors.
AI answers vary from run to run, even for identical prompts, and even on the same day. Collect data daily, which is where dedicated tools can help. Tools collecting data daily build a larger sample. Monthly reporting smooths out day-to-day variation and shows the actual trends. HubSpot AEO runs tracked prompts across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini daily , so marketers can review how brand visibility, sentiment, and citations change over time.
Important note: Teams should encourage delaying bigger decisions, such as rewriting pages or replacing prompts, for monthly or quarterly reviews. Patterns should be established over several weeks before implementing changes. It’s also important not to react to every drop. Sometimes a decline is industry-wide, and the best response is to wait rather than take action.
HubSpot’s free AI Search Sensor tracks daily answer engine volatility across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, along with weekly industry-level traffic, visibility, and citation trends. When a brand’s own metrics drop, the volatility score helps show whether the engines shifted across the market or the change is more likely specific to the brand. That context is useful for stakeholder reporting too: it can explain a dip that affected the whole industry, or show that a brand held steady while the industry declined.
The image above shows an industry-wide visibility score in the financial services industry. Three major players in the industry dropped in September at the same time, pointing to a change in how answer engines sourced or generated responses, not a problem with any single brand’s AEO strategy.
The prompts that prove business impact are the ones closest to revenue: prompts that lead to pages that convert, influence shortlists, or affect deals the business is already trying to win. Tracking these prompts gives marketers a way to connect AI visibility to outcomes leadership cares about, rather than reporting visibility for its own sake. The prompt types below make the strongest case for marketing’s direct impact on business.
Ongoing reporting needs prompts that stay stable over time, because it’s trends that help identify performance. Page-level fixes need prompts tied closely enough to specific pages that changes can be measured. The best prompts do both.
Pro tip: When fixing pages with AI writing tools, AI brand voice training helps keep updates consistent with the rest of the site.
AI prompt analytics show visibility. Proving impact means connecting visibility to what happens next. HubSpot AEO measures brand visibility, competitor mentions, sentiment, and citations from collected answers , and those metrics become more persuasive when paired with these signals.
HubSpot’s guide to content performance covers how to measure page-level results, which pairs well with prompt-level visibility data.
Pro tip: Report impact at the cluster level, not prompt by prompt. Individual prompts fluctuate, but a cluster’s visibility, traffic, and conversions moving together are a far more convincing story for stakeholders.
Prompt sets drift out of date as products, markets, competitors, and buyer language change. A quarterly review keeps prompt management manageable and keeps the set aligned with the business without disrupting trend data.
Pro tip: Schedule the prompt review after quarterly business planning. New priorities, product launches, and target segments are already decided by then, so the prompt set can be updated to match.
HubSpot AEO is available with Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise or as a standalone subscription. Configuring prompt tracking takes just a few minutes.
Five to 10 prompts per priority topic, across three to five topics, gives a starting set of 25 to 50 prompts, which is enough to spot patterns without creating noise. Use one or two representative prompts per intent cluster rather than many rewordings of the same question.
Review the prompt set quarterly and replace as needed, but maintain as much as possible because marketing analysis needs trend data to be comparable. Add prompts sooner when the business launches a product, enters a new market, or starts losing deals to a new competitor.
ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, Gemini, and Perplexity cover most AI search activity. HubSpot’s State of AEO found that consumers’ preferred platforms are ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews. The right mix depends on the audience, so check AI referral traffic in analytics to see which engines actually send visitors.
No. Track the full core set in the markets that drive the most revenue or growth, and a smaller, localized subset in secondary markets.
The most useful prompt sets aren’t the biggest; they’re a focused sample of unbranded, competitor, and branded prompts, weighted toward the research and evaluation stages where shortlists form, and ideally grounded in CRM and sales data.
Buyers are already making early decisions inside answer engines. Brands that aren’t visible at that stage may never make the shortlist. HubSpot AEO gives marketers one place to manage prompts, monitor visibility across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini, compare competitors, and turn citation gaps into prioritized content actions.

title: Ahrefs Brand Radar vs. Profound: Which fits your team?
content:
Marketers choosing between Ahrefs Brand Radar and Profound are really asking whether AI visibility belongs in your SEO suite or in a dedicated AEO platform. Brand Radar is the first option, Profound is the second, and HubSpot AEO is a third worth testing if you want visibility data connected to content and marketing workflows.
Brand Radar is enough for most Ahrefs-first teams. Profound earns its price when you need specialist depth, and HubSpot AEO fits teams that want tracking and next steps in one place. Below, we compare all three on engines, prompts, citations, sentiment, and price.
The connected case is simple. Tracking tells you where you’re missing, and recommendations tell you what to publish. HubSpot AEO covers both — start free below.
AI visibility tools measure brand presence, mentions, citations, sentiment, and competitive share in answer engines. Traditional rank trackers can’t fully measure brand presence in AI-generated answers, because there’s no fixed position to track. That gap matters. A 2025 Pew Research Center analysis of 900 U.S. adults’ browsing found users clicked a traditional result link in 8% of visits that showed a Google AI summary, versus 15% of visits without one. When fewer people click, being named inside the answer carries more weight.
The three tools come from different places. Ahrefs Brand Radar is an AI visibility feature associated with the Ahrefs SEO workflow. Profound is a dedicated AEO and AI intelligence platform. HubSpot AEO is a visibility tracker with recommendations, and it connects to the HubSpot platform. If you’re still mapping the landscape, our guide to AI search engines covers how each engine sources its answers.
Brand Radar’s biggest draw is its data source. Ahrefs builds its prompt database from real keywords, expands them into natural questions using People Also Ask and semantic fanout, then runs them through each AI platform. Ahrefs’ help center cites more than 405 million search-backed prompts, and its product page cites 448 million or more. The figure has moved between first-party pages, so check the live number before you quote it.
HubSpot AEO covers similar ground from a different angle. It starts from your own company, competitors, and industry to suggest prompts, then turns the results into recommendations. Pair either approach with our competitor research tools roundup if you also need classic traffic benchmarking.
Profound is built for AEO from the ground up. Its platform runs daily prompt analysis and layers on modules that SEO suites don’t match.
If you want the same kind of tracking with CRM context, HubSpot AEO in Marketing Hub Pro and Enterprise uses your CRM data to suggest prompts. For more on how sentiment gets scored across tools, see our roundup of sentiment analysis tools .
Pricing and plan details as of October 2026. Sources: Ahrefs product page and help center, Profound pricing page, HubSpot AEO product page, and the research brief’s facts document. Vendors change plans often, so confirm before you buy.
Your existing stack should drive the decision more than any feature list.
HubSpot AEO makes the most sense when measurement is only the first step. The workflow runs from visibility, to recommendations, to content and campaign action, to measurable marketing outcomes.
On its own, HubSpot AEO tracks your brand visibility score, competitor share of voice, citations, and sentiment across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, then turns gaps into prioritized recommendations such as creating a page, updating a post, or pitching an outlet. It costs $50 a month ($45 billed annually) and doesn’t require a HubSpot subscription or HubSpot CMS.
AEO in Marketing Hub Pro and Enterprise goes further. It uses your CRM data to suggest prompts, and it lets you act on recommendations in HubSpot’s content and social tools, with one-click blog drafts in your brand voice. That’s where the connected workflow pays off, because AEO data and campaign metrics live in one place. If you’re weighing how that fits a broader measurement plan, our guides to AI marketing analytics and brand tracking with AI show where AEO data slots in.
There are tradeoffs. HubSpot AEO tracks three engines, so teams that need AI Overviews, Copilot, or Claude coverage will need Brand Radar or Profound for those. It doesn’t offer server-log agent analytics or shopping modules either. For many inbound teams, the shorter path from insight to published content outweighs those gaps, and it’s easy to test.
Run the same evaluation on every tool so the results are comparable.
Then test the tool that matches your situation: Brand Radar if you already use Ahrefs, Profound if you need deeper specialist discovery, and HubSpot AEO for ongoing, connected measurement.
Pro tip: If you’re earlier in the evaluation, run HubSpot’s free AI Search Grader first. It’s a one-time snapshot of how ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini describe your brand, and it needs no account. Use it as a baseline, then move to continuous tracking.
As of October 2026, Ahrefs Brand Radar covers AI Overviews, AI Mode, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Copilot in its prompt index, with Claude available for custom prompts. Profound tracks three engines on its Trial and up to nine on Enterprise. HubSpot AEO tracks ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. Engine lists change often, so check each vendor’s page before buying.
Most teams don’t need both at the start. An SEO-suite feature like Brand Radar works well when you want AI visibility next to your existing SEO data. Add a specialist tool when you need capabilities the suite lacks, such as consumer prompt demographics, shopping analytics, or deeper crawler analysis. Start with one tool and a clear question, then add a second only when the first can’t answer it.
Turn each visibility gap into a content task with an owner and a date, then re-measure the same prompts after publishing. With AEO in Marketing Hub Pro and Enterprise, that loop happens inside HubSpot, because recommendations connect to content tools and campaign metrics sit beside AEO data. With other tools, you’ll move findings into your project tracker or CMS by hand or through integrations.
AI Search Grader is a free, one-time check of how ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini represent your brand. HubSpot AEO is ongoing monitoring that tracks specific prompts, compares competitors, and delivers prioritized recommendations. The Grader answers how AI represents you right now. HubSpot AEO answers how that’s changing and what to do next.
Take your 20 to 25 priority prompts and run them in each tool’s trial or demo. Compare how many your brand and competitors appear in, whether each tool’s engine list matches where your buyers search, and how easily you can export or share the results. Profound’s trial runs 50 prompts daily for 7 days, and HubSpot AEO lets you track 25 prompts at no cost to start. Ahrefs doesn’t offer free trials or discounts, so test with Custom Prompts inside an existing plan if you have one.
Brand Radar, Profound, and HubSpot AEO each solve a real problem. Pick Brand Radar when Ahrefs is your home base, Profound when you need specialist depth, and HubSpot AEO when you want measurement that leads straight to action.

title: 8 LLM visibility tools to track your brand across answer engines
content:
Large language model (LLM) visibility tools track brand mentions, citations, and share of voice across answer engines. According to Digitaloft , 80% of users rely on zero-click results at least 40% of the time, meaning they often get what they need directly from a search engine results page (SERP) or an AI-generated answer. That behavior can leave marketers with fewer on-site signals such as clicks, scroll depth, and engagement rate.
LLM visibility tools fill the measurement gap created by zero-click AI results by showing how often and how favorably a brand appears in AI-generated answers. Search engine optimization (SEO) metrics such as clicks, conversions, and keyword position still matter. Answer engine optimization (AEO) adds another layer of measurement by tracking repeated prompts, citations, sentiment, and competitor visibility across answer engines.
This roundup compares eight LLM visibility tools, from free diagnostics to enterprise platforms, so that marketers can evaluate the right fit for ongoing tracking.
LLM visibility tools measure whether and how a brand appears in AI-generated answers across answer engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews. Unlike traditional SEO rank tracking, these tools measure patterns across repeated AI responses rather than one fixed position. They typically record:
LLM visibility tools start with prompts modeled on questions people might ask while researching a category, problem, or product. The tool runs those prompts through its supported answer engines and records the responses.
A single manual check can show what an answer engine says at that moment, but reliable answer engine tracking requires repeatable prompts across multiple engines and time periods. The same prompt can return different answers between runs, so ongoing tracking tools repeat those checks on a schedule and measure patterns over time.
LLM visibility tools typically measure brand mentions, citations, sentiment, share of voice, competitor presence, and placement frequency depending on the platform. A mention within an AI tool looks like the following example:
The answer mentions five CRM brands, but none has a clickable citation. A citation includes a clickable link, and it looks like this:
A citation points readers to a source that was used or referenced in the generated answer. Citations can drive direct visits to websites, while unlinked mentions still contribute to a brand’s overall visibility.
Within the visibility tracking section, these tools measure two key dimensions: visibility tracking shows whether and how often a brand appears in generated answers, while citation analysis shows which domains, URLs, and content types appear as sources.
Marketers can compare LLM visibility tools across six practical criteria: engine coverage, prompt management, citation insights, competitor views, reporting, and workflow fit.
Engine coverage refers to which answer engines a tool tracks and whether those engines match the places a brand wants to monitor. Coverage can vary by plan, so marketers should compare what is included at the entry tier with what requires an upgrade.
For example, HubSpot AEO tracks ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. Profound tracks ChatGPT on its Starter tier, three answer engines on the Growth tier, and up to nine on the Enterprise tier.
Prompt management covers how teams add, edit, organize, and refresh the questions they track. Some products suggest prompts automatically, while others rely more heavily on manual setup.
Teams should also check what informs those prompt suggestions. Standalone HubSpot AEO uses company, competitor, and industry context, while AEO in Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise can use CRM data to surface prompts relevant to actual buyers.
Citation analysis shows which domains, URLs, and content types appear as sources in AI-generated answers. That information can help marketers identify owned-content gaps, third-party publications worth monitoring or pitching, and competitors whose content appears frequently.
Competitor reporting shows how a brand’s visibility compares with other companies for the same or related prompts. Depending on the tool, comparisons can include share of voice, prompt-level visibility, citations, sentiment, and changes over time.
Reporting options determine how easily teams can export or combine AI visibility data with other marketing data. Teams that need to move results into business intelligence tools or internal dashboards should check whether the plan they intend to buy offers exports or API access.
Workflow fit describes what happens after a tool identifies a visibility gap. Some products primarily report what happened; others add recommendations, optimization workflows, or content tools.
HubSpot AEO combines ongoing visibility, citation, competitor, sentiment, and recommendation data. AEO in Marketing Hub adds CRM-informed prompt suggestions and connects AEO insights with HubSpot’s broader marketing workflow for Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise customers.
The table below compares all eight tools on those criteria, so marketers can shortlist the right fit for their AI search tracking program before reading the individual write-ups.
The tools below take different approaches to AI visibility, from standalone tracking platforms to products that combine answer-engine data with broader SEO or marketing workflows.
HubSpot AEO is HubSpot’s ongoing answer-engine visibility product. Its standalone version tracks prompts daily across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity and reports brand visibility, sentiment, competitor share of voice, citations, and recommendations. Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise include AEO with additional CRM context.
HubSpot offers AI Search Grader , a free, one-time diagnostic check that evaluates how ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity represent a brand before teams commit to ongoing tracking. It scores five areas:
AI Search Grader is a snapshot, not an ongoing tracking product. It can give teams a baseline view before they commit to a recurring measurement workflow.
HubSpot’s case study on its own AEO program shows how HubSpot’s marketing team built an answer-engine measurement system around visibility, share of voice, and citations. For teams already using Marketing Hub SEO Marketing Software , AEO complements rather than replaces traditional search analysis. HubSpot’s SEO tools provide search recommendations, topic planning, reporting, and Google Search Console integration, while HubSpot AEO measures visibility inside answer engines.
Best for: Teams that want ongoing AEO monitoring, especially existing HubSpot customers that can use the deeper Marketing Hub integration.
Pricing: Standalone HubSpot AEO costs $50/month or $45/month when billed annually after a 28-day free trial. It is included with Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise. AI Search Grader is free.
What we like: AI Search Grader is free, and I put every client and their key competitors through it as a first pass because it gives an immediate diagnostic. For ongoing tracking, I like that HubSpot AEO brings visibility, citations, sentiment, competitors, and recommendations into one workflow. Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise add the CRM-informed prompts I find most useful for grounding tracking in actual business context. I also like that AEO can sit alongside HubSpot’s SEO tools and Google Search Console data rather than being treated as a replacement for traditional search analysis.
Semrush combines traditional SEO workflows with AI Visibility in Semrush One, allowing teams to monitor conventional search and answer-engine visibility in the same product family.
Best for: Teams already using Semrush that want traditional SEO and AI visibility in one workspace.
Pricing: Starter, $199/month or $165.17/month billed annually; Pro+, $299/month or $248.17/month billed annually; Advanced, $549/month or $455.67/month billed annually.
What we like: Semrush has been a long-standing tool in my arsenal, and I’d be lost without it. I like that Semrush One puts answer-engine visibility next to the SEO data I already use, so teams can compare both channels without stitching together separate platforms.
Profound is an answer-engine visibility platform that combines brand monitoring with prompt-demand data and enterprise reporting. Self-service plans start with narrower engine coverage, while the Enterprise plan expands to up to nine answer engines.
Best for: Enterprise teams that need broader engine, company, and regional coverage.
Pricing: Starter, $99/month billed yearly; Growth, $399/month billed yearly; Enterprise, pricing available on request.
What we like: We like that Profound pairs visibility monitoring with Prompt Volumes instead of treating every tracked question as equally important. Its broader engine and regional coverage also give larger organizations room to expand beyond a basic three-engine monitoring setup.
Peec AI is a standalone AI search analytics platform focused on brand visibility, competitor performance, citations, sentiment, and next steps.
Best for: Teams that want dedicated AI-search analytics without buying a broader SEO suite.
Pricing: Starter, $95/month; Pro, $245/month; Advanced, $495/month; Enterprise, pricing available on request. Annual billing receives a 15% discount.
What we like: We like Peec AI’s focused approach to AI visibility and its Actions workflow, which moves beyond reporting by giving teams a prioritized set of visibility and source opportunities to investigate.
Tracksuit is an always-on brand tracking platform that measures how consumers perceive a brand and its competitors. Unlike answer-engine visibility tools, Tracksuit does not track AI-generated answers directly. Instead, it provides consumer brand-health data showing how awareness, consideration, preference, usage, and brand associations compare across a category, which can complement answer-engine visibility data.
Best for: Brands that want always-on consumer brand-health and competitor tracking as a complement to answer-engine visibility data.
Pricing: Tracksuit starts at $19,500 per brand per year. Multi-brand and multi-market commitments may use different commercial models, and exact pricing requires a demo.
What we like: Tracksuit gives marketers a consumer-research counterpoint to answer-engine visibility data. It can help teams compare what AI systems say about a brand with how consumers actually perceive it. At the same time, social listening tools add another view of how audiences discuss the brand across public channels.
Rankshift is an AI visibility platform that tracks how brands appear across answer engines and combines visibility reporting with competitor, citation, crawler, and content-analysis tools.
Best for: Teams that want broad engine coverage, flexible prompt frequency, and generous project and user limits.
Pricing: Starter costs $82/month billed annually. Professional costs $189/month billed annually. Business costs $425/month billed annually. Enterprise pricing is available on request.
What we like: Rankshift combines broad engine coverage with flexible prompt frequency, citation analytics, and unlimited projects and users instead of reserving those basics for an enterprise tier.
ZipTie is an AI search intelligence platform that monitors brand mentions, citations, sentiment, competitors, and full responses across seven AI search engines. ZipTie’s pricing is configurable by engine coverage, prompt volume, and tracking frequency.
Best for: Teams that want to customize the engines, prompts, and tracking frequency they pay for.
Pricing: ZipTie uses usage-based pricing. Its current presets start at $35.63/month for Starter, $549.67/month for Professional, and $2,614.34/month for Enterprise. Teams can adjust those configurations, and annual billing discounts the prompt subtotal by 20%.
What we like: ZipTie lets teams configure engine coverage and tracking cadence instead of forcing every customer into the same fixed bundle. Its combination of visibility, sentiment, citations, competitor data, and action-oriented analysis also makes the reporting easier to connect with content work.
Gumshoe is an AI search management platform built around persona-based Visibility Audits. Gumshoe tests prompts across multiple models, shows which brands and competitors appear, and lets teams examine the citations and context behind those answers.
Best for: Teams that want to analyze AI visibility by buyer persona and topic rather than using one flat prompt list.
Pricing: Starter costs $99/month. Pro starts at $299/month.
What we like: We like Gumshoe’s emphasis on the context behind a visibility score. Persona, model, citation, topic, and competitor views make it easier to see where a brand’s results differ instead of treating every AI answer as part of one undifferentiated average.
AI visibility tracking for beginners is best managed as a staged rollout. A marketing team that tries to monitor every prompt across every platform on day one usually ends up with data nobody reviews. The sequence below builds a baseline in four weeks, starting with a free snapshot and moving into ongoing monitoring.
A prompt set is the group of questions a team tracks to see how answer engines represent a brand during research and buying decisions. When building your prompt set, start with prompts that reflect meaningful buyer questions rather than trying to maximize the number of prompts. Use several prompt types so the set covers different stages of discovery:
Source the wording from real audience inputs where possible. Sales-call transcripts, support tickets, search-query data, and social listening tools can all surface language customers already use. The right number of prompts depends on the product’s limits, the markets being tracked, and how broad the buying journey is.
Before making answer-engine optimization (AEO) changes to your content or strategy, capture a baseline measurement of your current visibility. HubSpot’s AI Search Grader can provide a free one-time diagnostic of how answer engines characterize a brand across dimensions such as sentiment, recognition, presence quality, share of voice, and competitive position.
Treat that result as a snapshot, not an ongoing measurement system. Once the team chooses a tracking platform, record the first results for the exact prompt set it will monitor. Those prompt-level results provide the baseline for measuring later changes in visibility, citations, sentiment, and competitor performance.
Mentions show when a brand appears in an answer, while citations show which domains or URLs the answer engine references as sources. Review the citations across your tracked prompt set and separate them into three categories: owned sources your brand controls, third-party sources from other publishers, and prompts where your brand does not appear.
Owned pages that already receive citations can reveal useful topics or formats to develop further. Third-party citations can identify publications, review sites, communities, or comparison pages where earned visibility may matter. Prompts where the brand does not appear can identify content or distribution gaps. The same fundamentals used to increase visibility for existing blog content can inform that work, while AEO adds the answer-engine-specific citation layer.
Prioritize changes by business relevance, the size of the visibility gap, and the team’s ability to act. Correct factual information the brand controls, review important third-party sources, and create or update owned content where the prompt and citation data show a meaningful gap.
A one-time audit cannot show whether visibility changes over time, so ongoing tracking requires repeated measurements. HubSpot AEO runs tracked prompts daily across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, and HubSpot recommends evaluating results across multiple days or weeks instead of drawing conclusions from isolated daily changes.
For Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise customers, AEO in Marketing Hub adds CRM-informed prompt suggestions and places AEO insights alongside other marketing data. Teams can compare those results with the sales KPIs they already report while treating AI visibility as one input in the measurement path to leads and pipeline rather than claiming complete attribution for zero-click AI influence.
Market-level context can also help explain sudden changes. HubSpot’s free AI Search Sensor tracks industry-level AI visibility and answer-engine volatility. It does not report a specific brand’s visibility, but it can help marketers see whether a change coincides with broader movement across AI search.
Prioritize the answer engines that matter to the business and that your chosen tracking platform supports. Keep in mind that while analytics tools can show visits arriving from AI platforms through referral traffic, they cannot measure people who see your brand in an AI answer but never click through—another reason visibility monitoring matters beyond click-based metrics.
For broad coverage, teams commonly monitor major surfaces such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, and Google AI Mode, then refine the mix as they collect their own audience and referral data.
No universal prompt count guarantees a reliable result. A useful prompt set should cover the buyer questions, products, use cases, competitors, and markets the team actually needs to understand.
Start with a focused prompt set that fits your chosen tool’s plan limits, then expand to additional prompts only when those new prompts answer distinct business questions about different buyer segments, products, use cases, or competitors — rather than adding volume for its own sake.
Yes, but the limits vary by product and plan. Some platforms include multiple projects, regions, or countries on self-service tiers, while others reserve expanded geographic or multi-brand tracking for higher tiers or custom plans.
Check the number of projects, supported locations, languages, models, and prompt allowances before choosing a plan.
Start by measuring AI-referred sessions, conversions, and contact-source data from your CRM, then compare those outcomes with visibility trends in your AEO tool. This approach creates a measurement path from AEO activity toward leads and pipeline without assuming every zero-click AI interaction directly caused a conversion.
AEO in Marketing Hub adds CRM-informed prompt suggestions and places AEO insights alongside marketing data. Standalone HubSpot AEO provides ongoing visibility tracking without requiring another HubSpot subscription.
Individual responses can vary between runs, which is why visibility tools repeat prompts on a schedule rather than relying on single measurements. Unlike traditional search rankings, AI-generated answers fluctuate between runs, so avoid treating a single answer as a durable position.
Repeated tracking can reveal directional patterns across a prompt set. HubSpot, for example, runs its tracked prompts daily and recommends reviewing performance over multiple days or weeks before evaluating trends.
AI-generated answers now sit alongside traditional search during product discovery and research. That makes AI visibility worth measuring, while the clicks, conversions, rankings, and other SEO metrics marketers already use remain important.
Teams that want ongoing monitoring can start with HubSpot AEO, which tracks prompts across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity and adds citation, competitor, sentiment, and recommendation data. Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise customers can use the deeper CRM-informed version inside Marketing Hub.
For teams that want to understand their current position before setting up ongoing tracking, HubSpot’s AI Search Grader provides a free one-time snapshot.
